title: A majority rewritten as "half, rounded up" lets two quorums miss each other
summary: The property that every quorum system rests on is that two majorities always share a node. The module states it next to the code, as `2 * majority(n) > n`, and the build proves it for every cluster size with a bounded model checker. A developer simplifies `n / 2 + 1` to `(n + 1) / 2`, which agrees on every odd size the tests use. The prover answers with n = 2: two "majorities" of one node each, which need not overlap.

change.description: Replace `n / 2 + 1` with `(n + 1) / 2`, "half rounded up", which reads as the definition of a majority. For 1, 3, 5 and 7 nodes, the sizes in the tests, both give the same answer.

risk: Clusters are run with even sizes more often than one would like: during a rolling resize from three to five nodes, after one node of a three-node cluster is removed, in two-node test environments that are then promoted. With this change a four-node cluster needs two votes to elect a leader, so two disjoint pairs can elect two leaders in the same term, and two writes acknowledged by two disjoint "majorities" can both be committed. Every safety argument in the protocol layer above is void, and nothing fails loudly: the cluster works until the day two partitions each hold exactly half of it.
explanation: The module's properties file states what `majority` guarantees: on every `n > 0`, `2L * result > n && result <= n`. The tool generates a harness that calls the method on a symbolic `n`, assumes the precondition and asserts the property, and JBMC searches for an `n` that violates it, over the whole 32-bit range after a pass over small values. It finds n = 2, for which the new code returns 1, and the tool replays the input on the method to show the result. The old code was proved to satisfy the property in the same way, over all 2^31 positive sizes; a property-based test would have sampled a few hundred of them. The property is written in `long` arithmetic on purpose: the first draft, `2 * result > n`, was itself refuted by the prover at n near 2^31, where the multiplication overflows.
resolution: Keep `n / 2 + 1`. The property stays in the properties file next to the code, and every later rewrite of this line, however obvious, is checked against it for every cluster size.
provenance: Constructed from a textbook simplification that is correct for every odd cluster size and wrong for every even one.

references.title: Howard, Malkhi and Spiegelman, Flexible Paxos: Quorum intersection revisited (why quorum intersection is the whole requirement)
